input.text: If you are a wood strawberry, your daughter plants grow more root over live substrate than over dead substrate, so you detect the state of a patch before you touch it. You also sense red and far-red light through a protein called phytochrome B. For nearly every other plant that borrows this row, nobody has measured whether you sense your neighbors by chemicals or by light.
input.note: Left out common dandelion's R1 (airborne volatiles from damaged neighbors): its quote gives no result. Far-red records for selfheal (R5) not tied to neighbors.

input.text: In the front eyes of the jumping spider Plexippus, cells sense ultraviolet and green only, and another jumping spider, Evarcha, could tell orange or blue stripes from all 26 shades of gray it was offered. In two garden spiders, Argiope bruennichi and Argiope amoena, the front eyes have a third kind of cell that senses blue. Nobody has measured which kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or whether you can tell colors apart.
input.note: Grade i for most species, so the row reports measured spiders and says plainly that your own species is unmeasured. Numbers like 360 nm left out because they have no job.

input.text: Most spiders have eight eyes, and only a few families, Dysderidae, Sicariidae and Oonopidae, have six, so you very likely have eight. The secondary eyes of spiders are regarded as motion detectors, and you very likely have some of these. Nobody has measured how your eyes are built or what each of them does for you.
input.note: Left out R1-R5 and R8 (single species or genus findings); R5 only applies to the Giant Lichen Orbweaver.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, the tapetum, a mirror-like layer at the back of your eye, reflects up to 130 times more light than the back of a human eye does, and you can detect light up to 7 times dimmer than a human can. Lions have a tapetum too, a milky blue one. Nobody has measured how faint a light a lion or most other cats can see.
input.note: Figures are from domestic cat only; the tapetum is recorded in lion but no dim-light threshold exists for other species.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and every insect in this group that has been measured sees far less fine detail than that. If you are a large white butterfly, you read about a quarter of a cycle a degree, if you are a drone fly about half a cycle, and if you are a common green darner dragonfly about 2. For most other species, including the monarch, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out interommatidial angles because the acuity figures already make the comparison.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, an African wildcat, an ocelot, a serval or a fishing cat, the pupil in the middle of each eye is a vertical slit. If you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, mountain lion or cheetah, your pupil is round. If you are a bobcat, a caracal, a Canada lynx or an Iberian lynx, it is nearly round, and if you are a Eurasian lynx, it is oval to diamond-shaped.
input.note: Species with grade g or i are not named; the row names only species with a measured pupil record. No record gives a reason for the shapes, so none is stated.

input.text: If you are a domestic dog, your eyes take in an estimated 240 degrees around you, where a human's take in about 180, and what both eyes see overlaps across roughly 30 to 60 degrees. You also have more rod cells than a human, even in the center of your retina where a human has none, and a layer called the tapetum behind the retina, which was full-sized in 7 of 10 dogs examined. Nobody has measured the field of view of most wild relatives such as foxes and jackals, and nobody has measured how any of you judge depth.
input.note: Left out the coyote night threshold (R3) and the dog and cat focusing range (R5, not a depth cue record) to keep the row short.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, you see most sharply in a small area toward the temple side of your retina, where one kind of color-sensing cell is packed densest. If you are a cheetah, that kind of cell forms a horizontal streak across your retina, as it does in other animals of open ground. Nobody has measured the sharpest spot in most other cats.
input.note: Left out the Spanish wildcat (R1): its cone density figure is a comparison with the domestic cat and had no job here.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, each of your eyes sees from straight out on its own side to 30 degrees past your nose on the other side. Wildcats, the jungle cat and the other cats of the genus Felis are relatives of the domestic cat, and you very likely have the same field if you are one of them. Nobody has measured the field of view in a lynx, a lion or any other cat outside that genus.
input.note: Left out R2 (140 degrees binocular): it does not fit R1's 30 degrees across the midline, which would give only about 60 degrees of overlap. Needs a check before use.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In honeybees, buff-tailed bumblebees, German wasps and several other bees and wasps, recordings from single cells found one kind of color-sensing cell that senses ultraviolet best. Nobody has measured how far into the ultraviolet your own cells reach.
input.note: Left out peak numbers (no comparison job). Dolichovespula norwegica (R14) lists only blue and green peaks, so I did not claim an ultraviolet cell for all wasps.

input.text: For most jumping spiders, nobody has measured how sharply you see. If you are a Phidippus johnsoni, your big front eyes see about an eighth of the detail a human sees, and you very likely share that with other Phidippus spiders. If you are a bold jumping spider, the light-sensing cells in the sharpest zone of each of your side eyes sit about half a degree apart.
input.note: R3's quote gives 0.13 degrees, not 3.8 cycles a degree; the eighth rests on the record value 3.8 against 30 for a human. R2 and R4/R5 left out.

input.text: If you are a red-winged blackbird, your two eyes together cover about 315 degrees of the circle around you, and about 50 degrees of that in front is seen by both eyes at once. If you are a mallard, each eye alone covers about 185 degrees, and the two eyes overlap by about 20 degrees. For most other birds, nobody has measured either width.
input.note: Left out a human comparison because no record gives a human field width.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all, and in the blue tit, the European starling and the Eurasian blackbird a cone cell senses it best at about 370 nanometers. If you are a songbird, you very likely sense ultraviolet too, and a blue tit's cornea and lens let it through. Birds are not all alike here: the mallard's cone of this kind peaks in violet, and in the pied cormorant the cornea and lens block ultraviolet.
input.note: Nothing is stated for turkey vultures or woodpeckers; ocular-media claims are kept to blue tit and pied cormorant by name.

input.text: Jumping spiders have eight simple eyes, and you very likely have eight as well. In the bold jumping spider, the two big front eyes can follow a moving target only with guidance from the smaller eyes at the side. Nobody has measured what each of your eyes does unless you are a bold jumping spider.
input.note: Left out the telephoto optics (R4, Plexippus validus only) and the vestigial rear eyes (R5, Lyssomanes only) to keep the row short.

input.text: Birds that have been measured differ widely in how sharply they see. A house sparrow sees about a sixth of the detail a human sees, a mallard about two fifths, and a magpie or a jackdaw about as much as a human. Nobody has measured how sharply most other birds see, so if you are none of these, your own sharpness is unknown.
input.note: No record gives interreceptor angle for any bird, so it is left out.

input.text: If you are a bold jumping spider, a low tone in the air makes you freeze, even when it comes from more than 3 meters away, and a shaking surface under your feet is unpleasant enough that you learn to avoid whatever you were looking at. If you are a brilliant jumping spider, the rate of a courting male's vibrations is an important part of whether he wins a mate. Nobody has measured what most other jumping spiders sense of sound or vibration.
input.note: Left out R1 (record names Corythalia canosa, list says Anasaitis canosa) and R3 (about courting signals sent, not sensed).

input.text: If you are a domestic dog with a long skull, like a wolf, you see most sharply along a band level with the horizon, and if you have a short nose, like a pug, you see most sharply in one spot in the middle. If you are a red fox or an Arctic fox, you have a sharp spot in the middle of the eye and a streak of sharper sight beside it. Nobody has measured this in the other species that share this view, so nobody knows which pattern you have.
input.note: Left out the ganglion and cone density figures because they stay with the red fox and Arctic fox and have no comparison job here.

input.text: If you are a honeybee, a buff-tailed bumblebee or a common eastern bumblebee, you see roughly a hundredth of the fine detail a human sees, as measured by training bees to tell stripes apart. Nobody has measured how sharply most other bees and wasps see.
input.note: Left out the giant hornet's estimate and all interommatidial angles, since they are anatomical estimates and the row needs one comparison. The human comparison uses the 30 cycles a degree figure from the brief.

input.text: Nobody has recorded an eye type for you. Nobody has measured whether any part of you forms an image of what is around you.
input.note: R1 covers moth and beetle eyes only, so I did not cite it. I left out "you have no eyes" and any light-sensing claim because no plant record supports them.

input.text: If you are a domestic dog, a red fox or an arctic fox, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where humans have three. In the domestic dog, one kind senses light most strongly at about 430 nanometers, a violet-blue, and the other at about 555 nanometers, a yellow-green.
input.note: Left out which colors look gray, since no record states it. Fox peak values cover only one pigment, so only the dog's two peaks are given.

input.text: If you are a bold jumping spider, each of the eyes just beside your two big front eyes sees about 70 degrees from side to side and about 100 degrees from top to bottom. The only other measurement is a side-to-side span of about 100 degrees for those eyes in Menemerus semilimbatus, a gray wall jumping spider's relative. Nobody has measured the rest, including how far the fields of your two eyes overlap.
input.note: Left out R8 (25 degree overlap, family-level, grade g) and R3/R4/R6/R7 (retina size of the front eyes, not a field of view); optics do not carry beyond the genus.

input.text: When something moves near you, you turn to face it. If you are a bold jumping spider, your big front eyes scan differently when dots move like a living animal than when they move in other ways. If you are a magnolia green jumping spider, the retinas of your side eyes are less refined for sensing motion than those of the other jumping spiders studied, and for most species nobody has measured how well you see movement.
input.note: Left out the turning speeds (R14) and the 16 degrees per second figure (R15): the records are for the family and the quotes do not name a species, so they cannot be pinned to one.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. One kind senses blue light most strongly and the other senses yellow-green light most strongly. Blue-sensing cells have also been found in the cheetah, the bobcat and the leopard, and nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell other cats have.
input.note: R3 is a dog measurement (429 nm), so I did not use it for any cat; the row gives no peak figures.

input.text: If you are a regal jumping spider, your big front eyes have three kinds of color-sensing cell, and one kind senses ultraviolet. If you are a Plexippus validus, you have only two kinds, green and ultraviolet, and if you are a Habronattus pyrrithrix, you have three, with the red-sensing kind in a small patch at the center of the eye. Nobody has measured how many kinds you have if you are any other jumping spider.
input.note: Left out the carried wavelength peaks and the 300-700 nm lens range because no number had a clear job; the orange/blue grating result (R12) is from Evarcha and was not stated.

input.text: You have no eyes, and for most plants nobody has measured how you sense light or what you do at each hour of the day. A few have been measured: common selfheal grows less under strong far-red light, English plantain grows larger under added ultraviolet-B, and Queen Anne's lace makes chlorophyll according to day length. For the hour of the day, chicory is one that has been measured, and its flower heads begin to open around sunrise.
input.note: No record covers how plants sense green light, so the row says nothing about green. Black locust, also measured for both traits, was left out for length.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. In the few spiders that have been measured, the answer varies a great deal: the big front eyes of a Portia jumping spider read about 12 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30, and the large night eyes of a net-casting spider called Dinopis read about a third of one. Those figures belong to those spiders alone.
input.note: No record covers any species or genus on the list, so no figure is carried; the row names only the measured spiders.

input.text: If you are a honeybee, you can see a light flicker even when it flashes 200 times a second, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. In the bumblebee Bombus hortorum the limit is about 130 flashes a second. Nobody has measured it in wasps, carpenter bees or most other bees.
input.note: Left out the impulse-response half-widths (R2, R3): they are in milliseconds, not flashes a second, so they give no flicker limit.

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see. In one crab spider, Xysticus cristatus, the front middle eyes stop seeing flicker at about 10 flashes a second, where a human stops at about 60. That figure belongs to that crab spider's eyes alone, and no one has measured it in your species.
input.note: Left out R2 (Cupiennius salei): its quote does not clearly state a flicker limit.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, you read about 10 cycles a degree, a third of the 30 that a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a cheetah, you read about 23, much closer to a human. Nobody has measured how sharply most other cats see, though wildcats of the same genus as the domestic cat very likely see about as sharply as it does.
input.note: Left out R3 (Panthera, qualitative only) and R4 (Lynx lynx 8, an unlabeled estimate), since neither supports a stated value.

input.text: Inside each of your two big front eyes, the retina moves, scanning across what you look at. If you are a bold jumping spider, your front eyes scan a still shape the same way with or without the eyes beside them, but they rely on those eyes to find and track a moving one. Nobody has measured this in most other jumping spiders, so nobody knows how closely you match the bold jumping spider.
input.note: Left out the fovea and the Marpissa priming and Salticidae dwell-time records to keep the row short and tied to the one measured species.

input.text: Unless you belong to one of the few species that have been tested, nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing it flicker. A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second. A blue tit still sees it at about 130, a European starling at about 100, a house sparrow at about 55 and a great horned owl at about 45.
input.note: Left out other measured species (hummingbird, flycatcher, cowbird) for length; the human figure of 60 comes from the brief.

input.text: A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and the eyes of the butterfly Danaus chrysippus, a relative of the monarch, still follow it at 165 to 210 flashes a second. Nobody has measured how fast your eyes follow a flicker unless you are in that genus or one of the few other species tested, and that figure stays with the species it was measured in.
input.note: Left out other species' flicker figures because they cannot travel to this view's other species; no record gives a speed for most of the 1,200 species.

input.text: If you are a domestic cat, what your two eyes see overlaps across about 140 degrees, the same as in a human, and you probably cannot focus on anything closer than about 25 centimeters. Nobody has measured the overlap or the closest focus in most other cats, including lions, lynxes and bobcats.
input.note: Left out R3 (blur of horizontal contours with a slit pupil): the quote does not state a depth cue or that every cat has a vertical slit.

input.text: If you are a golden silk spider, the insects caught in your web shake it 5 to 30 times a second, while air stirred by a flying insect seldom makes you attack and often makes you lift your forelegs. If you are a six-spotted fishing spider, you jump away from a striking frog, and the fine hairs called trichobothria that sense moving air are necessary and sufficient for that jump. For most other spiders, nobody has measured how you sense vibration or moving air.
input.note: Left out the orb weaver and web builder statements (R12-R14) because they are grade g and this row is graded i.

input.text: Monarchs, cabbage whites, small tortoiseshells and LD moths each have a color-sensing cell that senses ultraviolet best, and so do the drone fly, the seven-spotted ladybird, a dragonfly, a damselfly and the brown marmorated stink bug. You very likely have one as well. Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all.
input.note: No wavelength numbers used, since they have no comparison job here and do not carry between species.

input.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's. If you are a domestic dog, you see about a quarter of the fine detail a human sees. If you are a red fox, you read about 6 cycles a degree, and if you are an arctic fox, about 9, where a human reads about 30. Those are the only three species measured so far.
input.note: Dog figure is 20/75 Snellen (an estimate for a typical dog), turned into about a quarter of a human's 20/20. Red fox figure is inferred from ganglion cell maps.

input.text: Some spider eyes have a tapetum, a reflective layer behind the light-sensing cells, but in spiders it is always missing from the front middle pair. In two Argiope species the light-sensing cells of the eyes become more sensitive at night, and in the nocturnal Araneus ventricosus a front middle eye also follows a daily rhythm of sensitivity. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see, or whether your other eyes have a tapetum.
input.note: Left out the huntsman and lynx spider tapetum records and the Deinopis starlight record because the row is about most species; say if you want per-species rows.

input.text: Honey bees, bumblebees, wool carder bees and hornets each have three kinds of color-sensing cell, which sense ultraviolet, blue and green, and none of them has a cell for red. You very likely have no cell for red either, so red flowers and other red things look dark to you.
input.note: Left out the single-class records (R15, R18/R19, R20), which look like partial recordings. "Look dark" follows the approved example row and is not stated in any record.
